arXiv:cs/0603039v2 [cs.IT] 16 May 2006

Quantization Bounds on Grassmann Manifolds and Applications to MIMO Communications∗{}^{{}^{*}}

Wei Dai    Youjian Liu    Brian Rider Affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder Affiliation: 425 UCB, Boulder, CO, 80309, USA
Abstract

This paper considers the quantization problem on the Grassmann manifold 𝒢n,p\mathcal{G}_{n,p}, the set of all pp-dimensional planes (through the origin) in the nn-dimensional Euclidean space. The chief result is a closed-form formula for the volume of a metric ball in the Grassmann manifold when the radius is sufficiently small. This volume formula holds for Grassmann manifolds with arbitrary dimension nn and pp, while previous results pertained only to p=1p=1, or a fixed pp with asymptotically large nn. Based on this result, several quantization bounds are derived for sphere packing and rate distortion tradeoff. We establish asymptotically equivalent lower and upper bounds for the rate distortion tradeoff. Since the upper bound is derived by constructing random codes, this result implies that the random codes are asymptotically optimal. The above results are also extended to the more general case, in which 𝒢n,q\mathcal{G}_{n,q} is quantized through a code in 𝒢n,p\mathcal{G}_{n,p}, where pp and qq are not necessarily the same. Finally, we discuss some applications of the derived results to multi-antenna communication systems.

Index Terms:
the Grassmann manifold, rate distortion tradeoff, MIMO communications

I Introduction

The Grassmann manifold 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is the set of all pp-dimensional planes (through the origin) in the nn-dimensional Euclidean space 𝕃n\mathbb{L}^{n}, where 𝕃\mathbb{L} is either ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}. It forms a compact Riemann manifold of real dimension β​p​(n−p)\beta p\left(n-p\right), where β=1\beta=1 when 𝕃=ℝ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{R} and β=2\beta=2 when 𝕃=ℂ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{C}. The Grassmann manifold provides a useful analysis tool for multi-antenna communications (also known as multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems). For non-coherent MIMO systems, sphere packings of 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) can be viewed as a generalization of spherical codes [1, 2, 3]. For MIMO systems with partial channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT), which is obtained by finite-rate channel-state feedback, the quantization of beamforming matrices is related to the quantization on the Grassmann manifold [4, 5, 6].

The basic quantization problems addressed in this paper are the sphere packing bounds and rate distortion tradeoff. Roughly speaking, a quantization is a representation of a source in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). In particular, it maps an element in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) into a subset of 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), known as a code 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Define the minimum distance of a code δ≜δ⁡(𝒞)\delta\triangleq\delta\left(\mathcal{C}\right) as the minimum distance between any two codewords in the code 𝒞\mathcal{C}. A sphere packing bound relates the size of a code and a given minimum distance δ\delta. Rate distortion tradeoff is another important aspect of the quantization problem. A distortion metric is a mapping from the set of element pairs in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) into the set of non-negative real numbers. Given a source distribution and a distortion metric, the rate distortion tradeoff is described by the minimum expected distortion achievable for a given code size, or equivalently the minimum code size required to achieve a particular expected distortion.

There are several papers addressing the quantization problem for Grassmann manifolds. In [7], an isometric embedding of 𝒢n,p​(ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{R}\right) into a sphere in Euclidean space ℝ12​(m−1)​(m+2)\mathbb{R}^{\frac{1}{2}\left(m-1\right)\left(m+2\right)} is given. Then, using the Rankin bound in Euclidean space, the Rankin bound in 𝒢n,p​(ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{R}\right) is obtained. Unfortunately, this bound is not tight when the code size is large. Instead of resorting to an isometric embedding, sphere packing bounds can also be derived from analysis in the Grassmann manifold directly. Let B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) denote a metric ball of radius δ\delta in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). The sphere packing bounds can be derived from the volume of B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) [3]. The exact volume formula for a B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) with p=1p=1 and 𝕃=ℂ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{C} is derived in [4]. An asymptotic volume formula for a B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), where p≥1p\geq 1 is fixed and nn approaches infinity, is derived in [3]. Based on those volume formulas, the corresponding sphere packing bounds are developed in [5, 3]. Besides the sphere packing bounds, the rate distortion tradeoff is also treated in [8], where approximations to the distortion rate function are derived via the sphere packing bounds on the Grassmann manifold. However, the derived approximations are based on the volume formulas in [3, 4] which are only valid for some special choices of nn and pp: either p=1p=1 or fixed p≥1p\geq 1 with asymptotic large nn.

The main contribution of this paper is to derive a closed-form formula for the volume of a small ball in the Grassmann manifold. Based on this formula, sphere packing bounds are derived and rate distortion tradeoff are accurately quantified. Specifically:

  1. 1.

    An explicit volume formula for a metric ball in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is derived when the radius δ\delta is sufficiently small. It holds for Grassmann manifolds with arbitrary dimensions while previous results are only valid for either p=1p=1 or a fixed pp with asymptotically large nn. The main order term of the volume is cn,p,p,β​δβ​p​(n−p)c_{n,p,p,\beta}\delta^{\beta p\left(n-p\right)} for a constant cn,p,p,βc_{n,p,p,\beta} depending on nn, pp and β\beta. Lower and upper bounds on the volume formula are also derived.

  2. 2.

    Based on the volume formula, the Gilbert-Varshamov and Hamming bounds for sphere packings are obtained. For the distortion rate function, a lower bound is established via sphere packing argument and an upper bound is derived via random-code argument. The bounds are in fact asymptotically identical, and so precisely quantify the asymptotic rate distortion tradeoff. Since the upper bound is actually derived from the average distortion of random codes, it follows that random codes are asymptotically optimal.

  3. 3.

    The volume formula and the results on the rate distortion tradeoff are extended to a more general plane matching problem. In this plane matching problem, a plane from the code 𝒞⊂𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is chosen to match a random plane Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) to minimize the distortion, where pp and qq are not necessarily the same. For plane matching, a metric ball in 𝒢n,q​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) centered at a plane in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is studied. The volume formula is derived for such a ball with sufficiently small radius. The rate distortion tradeoff is also quantified by the same method as above.

  4. 4.

    As an application of the derived quantization bounds, the information rate of a MIMO system with finite-rate channel-state feedback and power on/off strategy is accurately quantified for the first time. Since the corresponding Grassmann manifold for most practical MIMO systems has p>1p>1 and small nn, the quantization bounds derived in this paper are necessary.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II provides some preliminaries on the Grassmann manifold. Section III derives the explicit volume formula for a metric ball in the Grassmann manifold. The corresponding sphere packing bounds are obtained and the rate distortion tradeoff is accurately quantified in Section IV. An application of the quantization bounds to MIMO systems with finite-rate channel-state feedback is detailed in Section V. Section VI contains the conclusions.

II Preliminaries

This section presents a brief introduction to the Grassmann manifold. A metric and a measure on the Grassmann manifold are defined, and the problems relevant to quantization on the Grassmann manifold are formulated. For completeness, we also extend the quantization problem to a more general plane matching problem.

II-A Metric and Measure on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right)

For the sake of applications [4, 5, 6], the projection Frobenius metric (chordal distance) is employed throughout the paper although the corresponding analysis is also applicable to the geodesic metric [3]. For any two planes P,Q∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P,Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), we define the principle angles and the chordal distance between PP and QQ as follows. Let 𝐮1∈P\mathbf{u}_{1}\in P and 𝐯1∈Q\mathbf{v}_{1}\in Q be the unit vectors such that |𝐮1†​𝐯1|\left|\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}_{1}\right| is maximal. Inductively, let 𝐮i∈P\mathbf{u}_{i}\in P and 𝐯i∈Q\mathbf{v}_{i}\in Q be the unit vectors such that 𝐮i†​𝐮j=0\mathbf{u}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}_{j}=0 and 𝐯i†​𝐯j=0\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}_{j}=0 for all 1≤j<i1\leq j<i and |𝐮i†​𝐯i|\left|\mathbf{u}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}_{i}\right| is maximal. The principle angles are defined as θi=arccos⁡|𝐮i†​𝐯i|\theta_{i}=\arccos\left|\mathbf{u}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}_{i}\right| for i=1,⋯,pi=1,\cdots,p [7, 9]. The chordal distance between PP and QQ is given by

dc​(P,Q)≜∑i=1psin2⁡θi.d_{c}\left(P,Q\right)\triangleq\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sin^{2}\theta_{i}}. (1)

The invariant measure μ\mu on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is defined as follows. Let O⁡(n)O\left(n\right) and U⁡(n)U\left(n\right) be the groups of n×nn\times n orthogonal and unitary matrices respectively. Let 𝐀,𝐁∈O⁡(n)\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in O\left(n\right) when 𝕃=ℝ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{R}, or 𝐀,𝐁∈U⁡(n)\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in U\left(n\right) when 𝕃=ℂ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{C}. For any measurable set ℳ⊂𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and arbitrary 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B},

μ⁡(𝐀​ℳ)=μ⁡(ℳ)=μ⁡(ℳ​𝐁).\mu\left(\mathbf{A}\mathcal{M}\right)=\mu\left(\mathcal{M}\right)=\mu\left(\mathcal{M}\mathbf{B}\right).

The invariant measure defines the uniform/isotropic distribution on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) as well [9].

II-B Quantization on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right)

Given both a metric and a measure on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), a quantization on the Grassmann manifold can be well defined. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a finite size discrete subset of 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). A quantization is a mapping from the 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) to the set 𝒞\mathcal{C} (also known as a code), i.e.,

𝔮:𝒢n,p​(𝕃)→𝒞.\mathfrak{q}:\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}.

An element in the code 𝒞\mathcal{C} is called a codeword. Thus, roughly speaking, a quantization is to use a subset of 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) to represent the whole space.

Sphere packing bounds relate the size of the code to the minimum distance among the codewords. Let δ\delta be the minimum distance between any two codewords of a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} and B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) be a metric ball of radius δ\delta in the 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). If KK is any positive integer such that K​μ​(B⁡(δ))<1K\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)<1, then there exists a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} of size K+1K+1 with minimum distance δ\delta. This principle is called as the Gilbert-Varshamov lower bound,

|𝒞|>1μ⁡(B⁡(δ)).\left|\mathcal{C}\right|>\frac{1}{\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)}. (2)

On the other hand, |𝒞|​μ​(B⁡(δ/2))≤1\left|\mathcal{C}\right|\mu\left(B\left(\delta/2\right)\right)\leq 1 for any code 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The Hamming upper bound captures this fact as

|𝒞|≤1μ⁡(B⁡(δ/2)).\left|\mathcal{C}\right|\leq\frac{1}{\mu\left(B\left(\delta/2\right)\right)}. (3)

For more information about the sphere packing bounds, see [3].

Rate distortion tradeoff is another important aspect of the quantization problem. A distortion metric is a mapping,

𝔡:𝒢n,p(𝕃)×𝒞→[0,+∞),\mathfrak{d}:\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right)\times\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\left[0,+\infty\right),

from the set of the element pairs in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and 𝒞\mathcal{C} into the set of non-negative real numbers. Throughout this paper, we define the distortion metric as the square of the chordal distance, 𝔡⁡(⋅,⋅)≜dc2​(⋅,⋅)\mathfrak{d}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)\triangleq d_{c}^{2}\left(\cdot,\cdot\right). Assume that a source QQ is randomly distributed in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). The distortion associated with a quantization 𝔮\mathfrak{q} is defined as

D≜E⁡[𝔡⁡(Q,𝔮⁡(Q))]=E⁡[dc2​(Q,𝔮⁡(Q))].D\triangleq\mathrm{E}\left[\mathfrak{d}\left(Q,\mathfrak{q}\left(Q\right)\right)\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[d_{c}^{2}\left(Q,\mathfrak{q}\left(Q\right)\right)\right].

The rate distortion tradeoff can be described by the infimum achievable distortion given a code size, which is called the distortion rate function, or equivalently the infimum code size required to achieve a particular distortion, which is called the rate distortion function. In this paper, the source QQ is assumed to be uniformly distributed in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). For a given code 𝒞⊂𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), the optimal quantization to minimize the distortion is given by11 1 The ties, i.e. the case that ∃P1,P2∈𝒞\exists P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathcal{C} such that dc​(P1,Q)=minP∈𝒞​dc​(P,Q)=dc​(P2,Q)d_{c}\left(P_{1},Q\right)=\underset{P\in\mathcal{C}}{\min}\;d_{c}\left(P,Q\right)=d_{c}\left(P_{2},Q\right), are broken arbitrarily as they occur with probability zero.

𝔮⁡(Q)=arg⁡minP∈𝒞​dc​(P,Q).\mathfrak{q}\left(Q\right)=\arg\;\underset{P\in\mathcal{C}}{\min}\;d_{c}\left(P,Q\right).

The distortion associated with this quantization is

D⁡(𝒞)\displaystyle D\left(\mathcal{C}\right) =\displaystyle= E⁡[minP∈𝒞​dc2​(P,Q)].\displaystyle\mathrm{E}\left[\underset{P\in\mathcal{C}}{\min}\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P,Q\right)\right].

For a given code size KK where KK is a positive integer, the distortion rate function is then given by22 2 The standard definition of the distortion rate function involves the code rate, which is log2⁡K\log_{2}K. The definition in this paper is equivalent to the standard one.

D∗(K)=inf𝒞:|𝒞|=KD(𝒞).D^{*}\left(K\right)=\underset{\mathcal{C}:\left|\mathcal{C}\right|=K}{\inf}\;D\left(\mathcal{C}\right). (4)

The rate distortion function is given by

K∗​(D)=infD⁡(𝒞)≤D​|𝒞|.K^{*}\left(D\right)=\underset{D\left(\mathcal{C}\right)\leq D}{\inf}\;\left|\mathcal{C}\right|. (5)

II-C An Extension: Plane Matching Problem

For the sake of completeness, we extend the quantization problem to a more general plane matching problem. The plane matching problem involves planes from different spaces 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and 𝒢n,q​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) where pp and qq are not necessarily the same.

To formulate the plane matching problem, we need to define the chordal distance between P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). Without loss of generality, we assume that p≤qp\leq q. Using the same procedure described in Section II-A, we are able to define the principle angles 0≤θ1≤⋯≤θp≤π20\leq\theta_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{p}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}. Based on the principle angles, the chordal distance between P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) are defined as dc​(P,Q)≜∑i=1psin2⁡θid_{c}\left(P,Q\right)\triangleq\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sin^{2}\theta_{i}}. In this way, the definition of chordal distance in (1) is just a particular case of the general definition.

Now consider the plane matching problem. Intuitively, the plane matching problem is to choose a plane from the code 𝒞⊂𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) to match a random plane Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) such that the average distortion is minimized, where 1≤p≤n1\leq p\leq n and 1≤q≤n1\leq q\leq n are not necessarily the same. Formally, a plane matching is a map from the whole space of Grassmann manifold, e.g., 𝒢n,q​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), to the code 𝒞⊂𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right),

𝔮:𝒢n,q​(𝕃)→𝒞,\mathfrak{q}:\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{C},

such that

D⁡(𝒞)≜EQ​[minP∈𝒞​dc2​(P,Q)]D\left(\mathcal{C}\right)\triangleq\mathrm{E}_{Q}\left[\underset{P\in\mathcal{C}}{\min}\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P,Q\right)\right]

is minimized. According to the same principles in the quantization problem, the rate distortion tradeoff can be extended to the plane matching problem.

III Metric Balls in the Grassmann Manifold

In this section, an explicit volume formula for a metric ball B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) in the Grassmann manifold is derived. It is the essential tool to quantify the rate distortion tradeoff in Section IV.

The volume calculation depends on the relationship between the measure and the metric defined on the Grassmann manifold. This paper focuses on the invariant measure μ\mu, which corresponds to the uniform/isotropic distribution, and the chordal distance dcd_{c}. For any given P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), define

BP​(δ)={Q^∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃):dc​(P,Q^)≤δ}B_{P}\left(\delta\right)=\left\{\hat{Q}\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right):\;d_{c}\left(P,\hat{Q}\right)\leq\delta\right\}

and

BQ​(δ)={P^∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃):dc​(P^,Q)≤δ}.B_{Q}\left(\delta\right)=\left\{\hat{P}\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right):\;d_{c}\left(\hat{P},Q\right)\leq\delta\right\}.

For the invariant measure μ\mu, it has been shown that μ⁡(BP​(δ))=μ⁡(BQ​(δ))\mu\left(B_{P}\left(\delta\right)\right)=\mu\left(B_{Q}\left(\delta\right)\right) and the value is independent of the choice of the center [9]. It is convenient to denote BP​(δ)B_{P}\left(\delta\right) and BQ​(δ)B_{Q}\left(\delta\right) by B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) without distinguishing them. Then, the volume of a metric ball B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) is given by

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=∫⋯∫∑i=1psin2⁡θi≤δ2​d​μ𝜽,\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=\underset{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sin^{2}\theta_{i}\leq\delta^{2}}{\int\cdots\int}\;d\mu_{\bm{\theta}}, (6)

where 1≤θ1≤π2,⋯,1≤θp≤π21\leq\theta_{1}\leq\frac{\pi}{2},\cdots,1\leq\theta_{p}\leq\frac{\pi}{2} are the principle angles and the differential form d​μ𝜽d\mu_{\bm{\theta}} is the joint density of the θi\theta_{i}’s, which is given in [9, 10, 11] and as well (20) in Appendix -A below.

The following theorem calculates the volume formula and expresses it as an exponentiation of the radius.

Theorem 1

When δ≤1\delta\leq 1, the volume of a metric ball B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) is given by

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=cn,p,q,β​δβ​p​(n−q)​(1+cn,p,q,β(1)​δ2+o⁡(δ2)),\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=c_{n,p,q,\beta}\delta^{\beta p\left(n-q\right)}\left(1+c_{n,p,q,\beta}^{\left(1\right)}\delta^{2}+o\left(\delta^{2}\right)\right), (7)

where

β={1if​𝕃=ℝ2if​𝕃=ℂ,\beta=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&\mathrm{if}\;\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{R}\\ 2&\mathrm{if}\;\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{C}\end{array}\right.,

Theorem 1 is of course consistent with the previous results in [4] and [3], which pertain to special choices of nn and pp and are stated below as examples.

Example 1

Consider the volume formula for a B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) where p=q=1p=q=1. Without normalization, the total volume of 𝒢n,1​(ℂ)\mathcal{G}_{n,1}\left(\mathbb{C}\right) is 2​πn/(n−1)!2\pi^{n}/\left(n-1\right)! and the volume of the B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) is 2​πn​δ2​(n−1)/(n−1)!2\pi^{n}\delta^{2\left(n-1\right)}/\left(n-1\right)! [4]. Therefore,

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=δ2​(n−1),\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=\delta^{2\left(n-1\right)},

agreeing with Theorem 1 where β=2\beta=2 and cn,1,1,2=1c_{n,1,1,2}=1.

Example 2

For the case that p=qp=q are fixed and n→+∞n\rightarrow+\infty, an asymptotic volume formula for a B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) is derived by Barg [3], which reads

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=(δp)β​n​p+o⁡(n).\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=\left(\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{p}}\right)^{\beta np+o\left(n\right)}. (10)

On the other hand, asymptotic analysis from Theorem 1 gives

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=(δp)β​p​(n−q)+O⁡(log⁡n)​(1−(β2​(q−p+1)−1)​δ2+o⁡(δ2))\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=\left(\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{p}}\right)^{\beta p\left(n-q\right)+O\left(\log n\right)}\left(1-\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\left(q-p+1\right)-1\right)\delta^{2}+o\left(\delta^{2}\right)\right)

for asymptotically large nn and any fixed 1≤p≤q1\leq p\leq q. The derivation follows the Stirling’s approximation applied to −1β​p​(n−q)​log⁡(cn,p,q,β)-\frac{1}{\beta p\left(n-q\right)}\log\left(c_{n,p,q,\beta}\right). In this setting, Theorem 1 is consistent with (10) and provides refinement.

Importantly though, Theorem 1 is distinct from the above results in that it holds for arbitrary pp, qq and nn. For a metric ball with parameter nn not asymptotically large, i.e., pp and qq are comparable to nn, it is not appropriate to use (10) to estimate the volume. A trivial example is that the p=q=np=q=n case. If p=q=np=q=n, the exact volume of B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) for ∀δ>0\forall\delta>0 is the constant 11. The formula in Theorem 1 gives cn,n,n,β=1c_{n,n,n,\beta}=1 and cn,n,n,β​δβ​p​(n−q)=1c_{n,n,n,\beta}\delta^{\beta p\left(n-q\right)}=1. However, the approximation (δ/n)β​n2\left(\delta/\sqrt{n}\right)^{\beta n^{2}} (formula (10)) will give a small number much less than 11 when δ\delta is small.

For engineering purposes, it may be satisfactory to approximate the volume of a metric ball B⁡(δ)B\left(\delta\right) by cn,p,q,β​δβ​p​(n−q)c_{n,p,q,\beta}\delta^{\beta p\left(n-q\right)} when the radius δ\delta is relatively small. Fig. 1 compares the exact volume of a metric ball (6) and the volume approximation cn,p,q,β​δβ​p​(n−q)c_{n,p,q,\beta}\delta^{\beta p\left(n-q\right)}. In the simulations, we always assume p=qp=q. The volume approximation becomes exact for the complex Grassmann manifold when δ≤1\delta\leq 1. To calculate the exact volume without appealing to Theorem 1, Monte Carlo simulation is employed to evaluate the complicated integrals in (6). Since

μ⁡(B⁡(δ))=Pr⁡{Q:dc​(P,Q)≤δ}\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right)=\Pr\left\{Q:\;d_{c}\left(P,Q\right)\leq\delta\right\}

where P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is chosen arbitrarily and QQ is uniformly distributed in the 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), simulating the event {Q:dc​(P,Q)≤δ}\left\{Q:\;d_{c}\left(P,Q\right)\leq\delta\right\} gives μ⁡(B⁡(δ))\mu\left(B\left(\delta\right)\right). The simulation results for the real and complex Grassmann manifolds are presented in Fig. 1(a) and 1(b) respectively. Simulations show that the volume approximation (solid lines) is close to the exact volume (circles) when the radius of the metric ball is not large. We also compare our approximation with Barg’s approximation (δ/p)β​n​p\left(\delta/\sqrt{p}\right)^{\beta np} (from (10)) for the case n=10n=10 and p=2p=2. Simulations show that the exact volume and Barg’s approximation (dash-dot lines) may not be of the same order while the approximation in this paper is much more accurate.

IV Quantization Bounds

This section derives the sphere packing bounds and quantifies the rate distortion tradeoff for both quantization problem and plane matching problem. The results developed hold for Grassmann manifolds with arbitrary nn, pp and qq.

IV-A Sphere Packing Bounds

The Gilbert-Varshamov and Hamming bounds for 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) are given in the following corollary.

Corollary 3

When δ\delta is sufficiently small (δ≤1\delta\leq 1 necessarily), there exists a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) with size KK and the minimum distance δ\delta such that

cn,p,p,β−1​δ−β​p​(n−p)​(1+O⁡(δ2))≤K.c_{n,p,p,\beta}^{-1}\delta^{-\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\left(1+O\left(\delta^{2}\right)\right)\leq K.

For any code with the minimum distance δ\delta,

K≤cn,p,p,β−1​(δ2)−β​p​(n−p)​(1+O⁡(δ2)).K\leq c_{n,p,p,\beta}^{-1}\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right)^{-\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\left(1+O\left(\delta^{2}\right)\right).
Proof:

The corollary is proved by substituting the volume formula (7) into (2) and (3). ∎

Remark 1

Applying Corollary 2 would provide sharper information on the higher order term. But we omit this.

IV-B Quantization: the Rate Distortion Tradeoff

The rate distortion tradeoff for quantization is characterized in this subsection33 3 For compositional clarity, the results for plane matching is summarized in a separate subsection IV-C.. Here, we assume that the quantization is on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), the source is uniformly distributed in 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and the distortion metric is defined as the square of the chordal distance. The derivation is based on the volume formula in (7). A lower bound and an upper bound on the distortion rate function are established. Denote the size of the code by KK. Then the lower and upper bounds are asymptotically identical when pp is fixed, nn and the code rate log2⁡K\log_{2}K approach to infinity with a fixed ratio. Therefore, these bounds precisely quantify the asymptotic rate distortion tradeoff. Note that the upper bound is the average distortion of random codes. Random codes are asymptotically optimal.

The following theorem gives a lower bound and an upper bound on the distortion rate function.

Theorem 2

When KK is sufficiently large ((cn,p,p,β​K)−2β​p​(n−p)≤1\left(c_{n,p,p,\beta}K\right)^{-\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}}\leq 1 necessarily), the distortion rate function is bounded as in

β​p​(n−p)β​p​(n−p)+2​(cn,p,p,β​K)−2β​p​(n−p)​(1+o⁡(1))≤D∗​(K)\displaystyle\frac{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)+2}\left(c_{n,p,p,\beta}K\right)^{-\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}}\left(1+o\left(1\right)\right)\leq D^{*}\left(K\right)
≤2​Γ​(2β​p​(n−p))β​p​(n−p)​(cn,p,p,β​K)−2β​p​(n−p)​(1+o⁡(1))\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\leq\frac{2\Gamma\left(\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\right)}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\left(c_{n,p,p,\beta}K\right)^{-\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}}\left(1+o\left(1\right)\right) (11)
Remark 2

For engineering purposes, the main order terms in (11) are usually accurate enough to characterize the distortion rate function. The details of the (1+o⁡(1))\left(1+o\left(1\right)\right) correction are spelled out in Theorem 3 below, where a quantization is viewed as a specific case of plane matching.

The lower bound and the upper bound are proved in Appendix -B and -C respectively. We sketch the proof as follows.

The lower bound is proved by a sphere packing argument. The key is to construct an ideal quantizer, which may not exist, to minimize the distortion. Suppose that there exists KK metric balls of the same radius δ0\delta_{0} packing and covering the whole 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) at the same time. Then the quantizer which maps each of those balls into its center gives the minimum distortion among all quantizers. Of course such an ideal packing may not exist. It provides a lower bound on the distortion rate function.

The basic idea behind the upper bound is that the distortion of any particular code is an upper bound of the distortion rate function and so is the average distortion of an ensemble of codes. Toward the proof, the ensemble of random codes 𝒞rand={P1,⋯,PK}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}=\left\{P_{1},\cdots,P_{K}\right\} are employed, where the codewords PiP_{i}’s are independently drawn from the uniform distribution on 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right). For any given code 𝒞rand\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}, the corresponding distortion is given by

D⁡(𝒞rand)=EQ​[minPi∈𝒞rand​dc2​(Pi,Q)],D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)=\mathrm{E}_{Q}\left[\underset{P_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\min}\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right)\right],

where Q∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) is a uniformly distributed plane. It is clear that D∗​(K)≤E𝒞rand​[D⁡(𝒞rand)]D^{*}\left(K\right)\leq\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\right]. We want to calculate E𝒞rand​[D⁡(𝒞rand)]\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\right]. Note that

E𝒞rand​[D⁡(𝒞rand)]\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\right] =\displaystyle= E𝒞rand​[EQ​[minPi∈𝒞rand​dc2​(Pi,Q)]]\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[\mathrm{E}_{Q}\left[\underset{P_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\min}\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right)\right]\right]
=\displaystyle= EQ​[E𝒞rand​[minPi∈𝒞rand​dc2​(Pi,Q)]].\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{Q}\left[\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[\underset{P_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\min}\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right)\right]\right].

Since 𝒞rand\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}} is randomly generated from the uniform distribution, E𝒞rand​[min⁡dc2​(Pi,Q)]\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[\min\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right)\right] should be independent of the choice of QQ. Therefore,

E𝒞rand​[D⁡(𝒞rand)]=E𝒞rand​[min⁡dc2​(Pi,Q)]\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\right]=\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[\min\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right)\right]

for any fixed QQ. By the volume formula and the extreme order statistics, we are able to calculate the distribution of dc2​(Pi,Q)d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right) (for ∀i\forall i) and min⁡dc2​(Pi,Q)\min\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P_{i},Q\right). In appendix -C, we prove that for any given Q∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), K2t⋅E𝒞rand​[D⁡(𝒞rand)]K^{\frac{2}{t}}\cdot\mathrm{E}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}}\left[D\left(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{rand}}\right)\right] converges to a constant as KK approaches infinity. Therefore, an upper bound of the distortion rate function is obtained for asymptotically large KK.

The rate distortion function is directly related to the distortion rate function. The following corollary quantifies the rate distortion function.

Corollary 4

When the required distortion DD is sufficiently small (D≤1D\leq 1 necessarily), the rate distortion function satisfies the following bounds,

1cn,p,p,β​(β​p​(n−p)2​Γ​(2β​p​(n−p))​D)−β​p​(n−p)2​(1+o⁡(1))≤K∗​(D)\displaystyle\frac{1}{c_{n,p,p,\beta}}\left(\frac{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}{2\Gamma\left(\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\right)}D\right)^{-\frac{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}{2}}\left(1+o\left(1\right)\right)\leq K^{*}\left(D\right)

To investigate the difference between the lower and upper bounds in (11), proceed as follows. Since the exponential terms are the same in both bounds, focus on the coefficients. Case 1

β​p​(n−p)=0\beta p\left(n-p\right)=0. This only occurs n=pn=p. Then the whole 𝒢n,n​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,n}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) contains only one element and no quantization is needed essentially.

β​p​(n−p)=1\beta p\left(n-p\right)=1. This happens if and only if 𝕃=ℝ\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{R}, n=2n=2 and p=1p=1. From here, the optimal quantization can be explicitly constructed. 12≤β​p​(n−p)β​p​(n−p)+2≤2β​p​(n−p)​Γ​(2β​p​(n−p))≤1,\frac{1}{2}\leq\frac{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)+2}\leq\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\Gamma\left(\frac{2}{\beta p\left(n-p\right)}\right)\leq 1,

and we expect the difference between the two bounds to decrease as nn approaches infinity. Indeed, the following corollary shows that the lower and upper bounds are asymptotically the same.

The lower and upper bounds asymptotically agreeing accurately quantifies the distortion rate function. Since the upper bound is actually derived from the average distortion of random codes, this implies that random codes are asymptotically optimal.

As a comparison, we cite the distortion rate function approximation derived in [8]. For 𝒢n,p​(ℂ)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{C}\right) with p=1p=1, that paper offers the approximation

D∗​(K)≈(n−1n)​K−1n−1D^{*}\left(K\right)\approx\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)K^{-\frac{1}{n-1}} (13)

by asymptotic arguments. According to our results in Theorem 2, the approximation (13) is indeed a lower bound for the distortion rate function and valid for all possible nn’s. For 𝒢n,p​(ℂ)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{C}\right) with pp fixed and n≫pn\gg p, a lower bound of an upper bound on the distortion rate function is given in [8] based on an estimation of the minimum distance of a code. It is less robust than the result in Theorem 2 in that it is neither a lower bound nor an upper bound, and it only holds for n≫pn\gg p (see Fig. 2 for an empirical comparison).

Besides characterizing the rate distortion tradeoff, we are also interested in designing a code to minimize distortion for a given code size KK. Generally speaking, it is computational complicated to design a code to minimize distortion directly. In [5] and [12], a suboptimal design criterion, i.e., maximization the minimum distance between codeword pairs, is proposed to reduce computational complexity. Refer this suboptimal criterion as max-min criterion. According to our volume formula (7), the same criterion can be verified. Let the minimum distance of a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} be δ\delta. Note that the metric balls of radius δ2\frac{\delta}{2} and centered at Pi∈𝒞P_{i}\in\mathcal{C} are disjoint. Then the corresponding distortion is upper bounded by

D⁡(𝒞)≤δ24​K​μ​(B⁡(δ/2))+p⁡(1−K​μ​(B⁡(δ/2))).D\left(\mathcal{C}\right)\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}K\mu\left(B\left(\delta/2\right)\right)+p\left(1-K\mu\left(B\left(\delta/2\right)\right)\right). (14)

Apply the volume formula (7). An elementary calculation shows that the first derivative of the upper bound is negative when

δ<4​β​p2​(n−p)2+β​p​(n−p).\delta<\sqrt{\frac{4\beta p^{2}\left(n-p\right)}{2+\beta p\left(n-p\right)}}.

This property implies the upper bound (14) is a decreasing function of δ\delta when δ\delta is small enough. Thus, max-min criterion is an appropriate design criterion to obtain codes with small distortion. Since this criterion only requires to calculate the distance between codeword pairs, the computational complexity is less than that of designing a code to minimize the distortion directly.

Fig. 2 compares the simulated distortion rate function (the plus markers) with its lower bound (the dashed lines) and upper bound (the solid lines) in (11). To simulate the distortion rate function, we use the max-min criterion to design codes and use the minimum distortion of the designed codes as the distortion rate function. Simulation results show that the bounds in (11) hold for large KK. When KK is relatively small, the formula (11) can serve as good approximations to the distortion rate function as well. Simulations also verify the previous discussion on the difference between the two bounds. The difference between the bounds is small and it becomes smaller as nn increases. In addition, we compare our bounds with the approximation (the “x” markers) derived in [8]. Simulations show that the approximation in [8] is neither an upper bound nor a lower bound. It works for the case that n=10n=10 and p=2p=2 but doesn’t work when n≤8n\leq 8 and p=2p=2. As a comparison, the bounds (11) derived in this paper hold for arbitrary nn and pp.

V An Application to MIMO Systems with Finite Rate Channel State Feedback

As an application of the derived quantization bounds on the Grassmann manifold, this section discusses the information theoretical benefit of finite-rate channel-state feedback for MIMO systems using power on/off strategy. In particular, we show that the benefit of the channel state feedback can be accurately characterized by the distortion of a quantization on the Grassmann manifold.

The effect of finite-rate feedback on MIMO systems using power on/off strategy has been widely studied. MIMO systems with only one on-beam are discussed in [4] and [5], where the beamforming codebook design criterion and performance analysis are derived by geometric arguments in the Grassmann manifold 𝒢n,1​(ℂ)\mathcal{G}_{n,1}\left(\mathbb{C}\right). MIMO systems with multiple on-beams are considered in [13, 14, 8, 15, 16]. Criteria to select the beamforming matrix are developed in [13] and [14]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) loss due to quantized beamforming is discussed in [8]. The corresponding analysis is based on Barg’s formula (10) and only valid for MIMO systems with asymptotically large number of transmit antennas. The effect of beamforming quantization on information rate is investigated in [15] and [16]. The loss in information rate is quantified for high SNR region in [15]. That analysis is based on an approximation of the logdet function in the high SNR region and a metric on the Grassmann manifold other than the chordal distance. In [16], a formula to calculate the information rate for all SNR regimes is proposed by letting the numbers of transmit antennas, receive antennas and feedback rate approach infinity simultaneously. But this formula overestimates the performance in general.

The basic model of a wireless communication system with LTL_{T} transmit antennas, LRL_{R} receive antennas and finite-rate channel state feedback is given in Fig. 3. The information bit stream is encoded into the Gaussian signal vector 𝐗∈ℂs×1\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times 1} and then multiplied by the beamforming matrix 𝐏∈ℂLT×s\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{C}^{L_{T}\times s} to generate the transmitted signal 𝐓=𝐏𝐗\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{PX}, where ss is the dimension of the signal 𝐗\mathbf{X} satisfying 1≤s≤LT1\leq s\leq L_{T} and the beamforming matrix 𝐏\mathbf{P} satisfies 𝐏†​𝐏=𝐈s\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}_{s}. In power on/off strategy, E⁡[𝐗𝐗†]=Pon​𝐈s\mathrm{E}\left[\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\dagger}\right]=P_{\mathrm{on}}\mathbf{I}_{s} where the PonP_{\mathrm{on}} constant denotes the on-power. Assume that the channel 𝐇\mathbf{H} is Rayleigh flat fading, i.e., the entries of 𝐇\mathbf{H} are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) circularly symmetric complex Gaussian variables with zero mean and unit variance (𝒞​𝒩​(0,1)\mathcal{CN}\left(0,1\right)) and 𝐇\mathbf{H} is i.i.d. for each channel use. Let 𝐘∈ℂLR×1\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{C}^{L_{R}\times 1} be the received signal and 𝐖∈ℂLR×1\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{C}^{L_{R}\times 1} be the Gaussian noise, then

𝐘=𝐇𝐏𝐗+𝐖,\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{HPX}+\mathbf{W},

where E⁡[𝐖𝐖†]=𝐈LRE\left[\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\dagger}\right]=\mathbf{I}_{L_{R}}. We also assume that there is a beamforming codebook ℬ={𝐏i∈ℂLT×s:\mathcal{B}=\left\{\mathbf{P}_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{L_{T}\times s}:\right. 𝐏i†𝐏i=𝐈s}\left.\mathbf{P}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}_{i}=\mathbf{I}_{s}\right\} declared to both the transmitter and the receiver before the transmission. At the beginning of each channel use, the channel state 𝐇\mathbf{H} is perfectly estimated at the receiver. A message, which is a function of the channel state, is sent back to the transmitter through a feedback channel. The feedback is error-free and rate limited. According to the channel state feedback, the transmitter chooses an appropriate beamforming matrix 𝐏i∈ℬ\mathbf{P}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}. Let the feedback rate be RfbR_{\mathrm{fb}}bits/channel use. Then the size of the beamforming codebook |ℬ|≤2Rfb\left|\mathcal{B}\right|\leq 2^{R_{\mathrm{fb}}}. The feedback function is a mapping from the set of channel state into the beamforming matrix index set, φ:{𝐇}→{i: 1≤i≤|ℬ|}\varphi:\;\left\{\mathbf{H}\right\}\rightarrow\left\{i:\;1\leq i\leq\left|\mathcal{B}\right|\right\}. This section will quantify the corresponding information rate

where Pon=ρ/sP_{\mathrm{on}}=\rho/s and ρ\rho is the average received SNR.

In this setting, the optimal beamforming matrix is given by 𝐏opt=𝐕s\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{opt}}=\mathbf{V}_{s} where 𝐕s∈ℂLT×s\mathbf{V}_{s}\in\mathbb{C}^{L_{T}\times s} is the matrix composed by the right singular vectors of 𝐇\mathbf{H} corresponding to the largest ss singular values [6]. Thus, the difference between perfect beamforming case (15) and finite-rate feedback case (17) is quantified by ηsup\eta_{\sup}, which depends on the distortion rate function on the 𝒢LT,s​(ℂ)\mathcal{G}_{L_{T},s}\left(\mathbb{C}\right). Substituting quantization bounds (11) into (18) and applying the asymptotic formula in [6] for E𝐇​[∑i=1sln⁡(1+c​λi)]\mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{H}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{s}\ln\left(1+c\lambda_{i}\right)\right] produce approximations of the information rate ℐ\mathcal{I} as a function of the feedback rate RfbR_{\mathrm{fb}}.

Simulations verify the above approximations. Let m=min⁡(LT,LR)m=\min\left(L_{T},L_{R}\right). Fig. 4 compares the simulated information rate (circles) and approximations as functions of Rfb/m2R_{\mathrm{fb}}/m^{2}. The information rate approximated by the lower bound (solid lines) and the upper bound (dotted lines) in (11) are presented. The simulation results show that the performances approximated by the bounds (11) match the actual performance almost perfectly. As a comparison, the approximation proposed in [16, 17], which is based on asymptotic analysis and Gaussian approximation, overestimates the information rate. Furthermore, we compare the simulated information rate and the approximations for a large range of SNRs in Fig. 5. Without loss of generality, we only present the lower bound in (11) because it corresponds to the random codes and can be achieved by appropriate code design. Fig. 5(a) shows that the difference between the simulated and approximated information rate is almost unnoticeable. To make the performance difference clearer, Fig. 5(b) gives the relative performance as the ratio of the considered performance and the capacity of a 4×24\times 2 MIMO achieved by water filling power control. The difference in relative performance is also small for all SNR regimes.

VI Conclusion

This paper considers the quantization problem on the Grassmann manifold. Based on an explicit volume formula for a metric ball in the 𝒢n,p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), sphere packing bounds are obtained and the rate distortion tradeoff is accurately characterized by establishing bounds on the distortion function. Simulations verify the developed results. As an application of the derived quantization bounds, the information rate of a MIMO system with finite-rate channel-state feedback and power on/off strategy is accurately quantified for the first time.

after some simplifications.

-A2 n2≤p≤q≤n\frac{n}{2}\leq p\leq q\leq n case

This computation is closely related to that for the 1≤p≤q≤n21\leq p\leq q\leq\frac{n}{2} case.

To see the connection between the n2≤p≤q≤n\frac{n}{2}\leq p\leq q\leq n and 1≤p≤q≤n21\leq p\leq q\leq\frac{n}{2} cases, we define the generator matrix and the orthogonal complement plane. For any given plane P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), the generator matrix 𝐏∈𝕃n×p\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{L}^{n\times p} is the matrix whose pp columns are orthonormal and expand the plane PP. The generator matrix is not uniquely defined. However, the chordal distance between P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) can be uniquely defined by their generator matrices. Indeed,

dc2​(P,Q)=min⁡(p,q)−tr⁡(𝐏†​𝐐𝐐†​𝐏),d_{c}^{2}\left(P,Q\right)=\min\left(p,q\right)-\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right),

where 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐐\mathbf{Q} are generator matrices for the plane PP and QQ respectively. It can be shown that the chordal distance is independent of the choice of the generator matrices. The orthogonal complement plane is defined as follows. For any given plane P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), its orthogonal complement plane P⟂P^{\perp} is the plane in 𝒢n,n−p​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,n-p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) such that the minimum principle angle between PP and P⟂P^{\perp} is π2\frac{\pi}{2}. It is straightforward that 𝐏†​𝐏⟂=𝟎\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}^{\perp}=\mathbf{0} where 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐏⟂\mathbf{P}^{\perp} are the generator matrices for PP and P⟂P^{\perp} respectively, and the matrix 𝟎\mathbf{0} is the p×(n−p)p\times\left(n-p\right) matrix with all elements 00.

With the definition of the orthogonal complement plane, the chordal distance between PP and QQ can be related to that between P⟂P^{\perp} and Q⟂Q^{\perp}. The relationship is given in the following lemma.

Lemma 2

For any given planes P∈𝒢n,p​(𝕃)P\in\mathcal{G}_{n,p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q∈𝒢n,q​(𝕃)Q\in\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right), let P⟂∈𝒢n,n−p​(𝕃)P^{\perp}\in\mathcal{G}_{n,n-p}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and Q⟂∈𝒢n,n−q​(𝕃)Q^{\perp}\in\mathcal{G}_{n,n-q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) be their orthogonal complement planes respectively. Then

dc2​(P,Q)=dc2​(P⟂,Q⟂).d_{c}^{2}\left(P,Q\right)=d_{c}^{2}\left(P^{\perp},Q^{\perp}\right).
Proof:

This lemma can be proved by the generator matrices. Let 𝐏\mathbf{P}, 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, 𝐏⟂\mathbf{P}^{\perp} and 𝐐⟂\mathbf{Q}^{\perp} be the generator matrices for PP, QQ, P⟂P^{\perp} and Q⟂Q^{\perp} respectively. Without loss of generality, we also assume that 1≤p≤q≤n1\leq p\leq q\leq n. Then

p\displaystyle p =\displaystyle= tr⁡(𝐏†​[𝐐∣𝐐⟂]​[𝐐∣𝐐⟂]†​𝐏)\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\left[\mathbf{Q}\mid\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right]\left[\mathbf{Q}\mid\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right]^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right)
=\displaystyle= tr⁡(𝐏†​𝐐𝐐†​𝐏)+tr⁡(𝐏†​𝐐⟂​(𝐐⟂)†​𝐏),\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right)+\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right),

where the matrix [𝐐∣𝐐⟂]\left[\mathbf{Q}\mid\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right] is the one composed of 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and 𝐐⟂\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}. Similarly,

n−q\displaystyle n-q =\displaystyle= tr⁡((𝐐⟂)†​[𝐏∣𝐏⟂]​[𝐏∣𝐏⟂]†​𝐐⟂)\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\left(\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\left[\mathbf{P}\mid\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\right]\left[\mathbf{P}\mid\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\right]^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)
=\displaystyle= tr⁡((𝐐⟂)†​𝐏𝐏†​𝐐⟂)+tr⁡((𝐐⟂)†​𝐏⟂​(𝐏⟂)†​𝐐⟂).\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\left(\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)+\mathrm{tr}\left(\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right).

Then

dc2​(P,Q)\displaystyle d_{c}^{2}\left(P,Q\right) =(a)\displaystyle\overset{\left(a\right)}{=} p−tr⁡(𝐏†​𝐐𝐐†​𝐏)\displaystyle p-\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right)
=\displaystyle= tr⁡(𝐏†​𝐐⟂​(𝐐⟂)†​𝐏)\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}\right)
=\displaystyle= n−q−tr⁡((𝐐⟂)†​𝐏⟂​(𝐏⟂)†​𝐐⟂)\displaystyle n-q-\mathrm{tr}\left(\left(\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\perp}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{Q}^{\perp}\right)
=(b)\displaystyle\overset{\left(b\right)}{=} dc2​(P⟂,Q⟂),\displaystyle d_{c}^{2}\left(P^{\perp},Q^{\perp}\right),

where (a) and (b) are from the definition of the chordal distance and the facts that min⁡(p,q)=p\min\left(p,q\right)=p and min⁡(n−p,n−q)=n−q\min\left(n-p,n-q\right)=n-q. ∎

By this lemma, the connection between the n2≤p≤q≤n\frac{n}{2}\leq p\leq q\leq n case and 1≤p≤q≤n21\leq p\leq q\leq\frac{n}{2} case is clear. The volume formula for the n2≤p≤q≤n\frac{n}{2}\leq p\leq q\leq n case can be calculated as follows.

=\displaystyle= Pr(Q⟂∈𝒢n,n−q(𝕃):dc2(P⟂,Q⟂)≤δ2)\displaystyle\Pr\left(Q^{\perp}\in\mathcal{G}_{n,n-q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right):\;d_{c}^{2}\left(P^{\perp},Q^{\perp}\right)\leq\delta^{2}\right)
=\displaystyle= μ​(BP⟂​(δ))\displaystyle\mu\left(B_{P^{\perp}}\left(\delta\right)\right)

where BP​(δ)B_{P}\left(\delta\right) and BP⟂​(δ)B_{P^{\perp}}\left(\delta\right) are the metric balls in 𝒢n,q​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) and 𝒢n,n−q​(𝕃)\mathcal{G}_{n,n-q}\left(\mathbb{L}\right) respectively. Therefore, the results for the 1≤p≤q≤n21\leq p\leq q\leq\frac{n}{2} case can be directly applied by letting p′=n−qp^{\prime}=n-q and q′=n−pq^{\prime}=n-p. Finally after some simplification, we have

where

cn,p,q,β=1Γ⁡(β2​p​(n−q)+1)​∏i=1n−qΓ​(β2​(n−i+1))Γ​(β2​(n−p−i+1)),c_{n,p,q,\beta}=\frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{2}p\left(n-q\right)+1\right)}\prod_{i=1}^{n-q}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\left(n-i+1\right)\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\left(n-p-i+1\right)\right)},

and

cn,p,q,β(1)=−(β2​(q−p+1)−1)​β2​p​(n−q)β2​p​(n−q)+1.c_{n,p,q,\beta}^{\left(1\right)}=-\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\left(q-p+1\right)-1\right)\frac{\frac{\beta}{2}p\left(n-q\right)}{\frac{\beta}{2}p\left(n-q\right)+1}.
